context: linear systems-led · trackform is the enabler, traction power & signalling drive the programme

brief.intro: New to this project type? Railway Track & Systems covers the length of a rail corridor — laying the track itself and installing everything that makes it operate: the overhead line that powers electric trains, the signalling that keeps trains apart, and the telecoms that tie it all together. Unlike a station or a building, there is no single site; progress is measured in track-kilometres, and work advances along the corridor as a moving front rather than through areas of one building. Civil trackbed and structure are largely an enabler, done early to a tight tolerance; the real programme risk sits in overhead-line (OCS/OHLE) energisation and signalling integration and testing, which typically run in a chain of scheduled possessions (track-access windows) late in the programme. Because trains only run once the whole line proves out together, sections finishing early still wait on the slowest system before line-wide dynamic testing can start.

scope.name: Formation & trackbed
scope.desc: Earthworks, subgrade preparation and drainage along the corridor.

scope.name: Trackform
scope.desc: Laying and aligning ballasted track or slab track to design geometry.

scope.name: OCS/OHLE structures
scope.desc: Mast foundations and erection of the overhead-line mast structure.

scope.name: Traction power (electrification)
scope.desc: Stringing OCS/OHLE contact and catenary wire, and installing feeder and sectioning stations.

scope.name: Signalling & train control
scope.desc: Trackside equipment, interlocking and train-detection that keep trains safely apart.

scope.name: Cabling & containment
scope.desc: Troughing routes and cable laying for power, signal and telecom systems.

scope.name: Earthing & traction return
scope.desc: Rail bonding and stray-current mitigation protecting buried structures from corrosion.

scope.name: Telecoms
scope.desc: GSM-R/radio coverage and the fibre-optic backbone connecting the line to the control centre.

scope.name: Lineside structures
scope.desc: Level crossings, signal bases and other lineside civil structures.

scope.name: Testing, integration & dynamic testing
scope.desc: Track geometry checks, systems integration and running trains at increasing speed to prove the line works together.

glossary.plain: Overhead Contact System / Overhead Line Equipment — the wires above the track that power electric trains.
the roof-mounted arm on a train that touches the overhead wire to draw power.
a scheduled period when a section of live or nearly-live track is closed so work can happen safely.
track laid on stone ballast (traditional, adjustable) versus track fixed to a continuous concrete slab (low-maintenance, less tolerant of error).
the signalling logic that physically prevents conflicting train movements.
the current that returns through the rails to the substation, and the corrosion risk if it strays into buried metal — controlled by bonding and earthing.
the dedicated radio system trains and control centres use to communicate.
the measured alignment, gauge and level of the finished track, checked against design tolerance.
running trains over the finished track and systems at increasing speed to prove everything works together.

must_get_right: This is a linear programme measured in track-kilometres, not areas — plan progress and resourcing as a moving front along the corridor, with a clear handback of each completed section.

Possessions/track-access windows are the scarce resource — electrification and signalling installation, testing and any rework can usually only happen in scheduled windows, so window allocation sets the real pace late in the programme, not generic trade productivity.

Signalling integration and dynamic testing are chain-linked — the whole line, or a defined section, must prove out together before any part carries trains, so the finish date is set by the slowest system, not the average.
Earthing and traction-return bonding are safety-critical and easy to under-scope — treat them as a first-class system, not an afterthought to the civil trackbed.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The network is structured by chainage/track-km section rather than by building area, and progress is measured per section.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Trackbed and civil works run a standard calendar; electrification and signalling installation and testing run inside allocated possessions/track-access windows (often night or weekend), which the calendar models explicitly rather than as generic working time.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs formation & trackform (by section) → OCS/OHLE mast erection & wire stringing → signalling trackside install → energisation → signalling integration → dynamic testing → handover. Possession-window availability, not trade productivity alone, usually paces the electrification and signalling fronts.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Trackbed is handed over to tolerance per section on a rolling basis; possession windows are allocated per the agreed access plan; interfacing systems (substations, control centre) are available for integration testing on schedule; a single electrification/signalling mobilisation.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Possession/track-access windows are the primary constraint on work; corridor access for plant (tamping machines, wiring trains) is linear and sequential; specialist signalling and OHLE commissioning engineers are a shared, scarce resource across the line.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: possession-window loss or curtailment, signalling software integration slippage, and OHLE wire-stringing rework from geometry non-conformance. Schedule contingency is held around energisation and the final dynamic-testing chain rather than spread across trackform activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by section/chainage; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead per possession — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
